name: Firestarter KDA Dance
tagline: Turns a single portrait or character image into a short looping dance video using a hosted video model.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; per-generation price and resolution tiers unverified.

verdictSummary: The product is a form, a prompt preset, and a queue in front of someone else's video model. An agent can rebuild the form, the preset, and the queue in an afternoon, and the output quality will be identical because it is the same model doing the work. What it cannot rebuild is the model itself: Seedance class image-to-video is not something you run on a laptop, so your personal version still rents inference from a provider like fal or Replicate and still pays per second of video. That makes the DIY build a markup-removal exercise rather than an independence exercise, which is a real win if you generate a lot and a pointless detour if you want three clips ever. Price it honestly against provider rates before you build.
coreLoopDIY: A local web page where you drop an image, pick 8s or 12s and 480p or 720p, fire a dance prompt at a hosted image-to-video endpoint, and watch the finished MP4 land in a local gallery.
requirements: A fal.ai or Replicate account with credits and an API key
Source images you actually have the rights to animate
Patience for 1 to 4 minute render times and occasional failed jobs
whatYouLose: Someone else absorbing failed or mangled generations instead of you paying for them twice
Prompt presets that have already been tuned against this specific model, which is most of the perceived quality
A content filter standing between you and a very bad decision about whose face you upload
A hosted URL that works from your phone without you running a dev server
Card-on-file checkout instead of topping up API credits
moatNotes: The model moat belongs to ByteDance, not to this site. The site's own edge is prompt tuning and not making you read API docs.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is signing up for an inference provider, reading endpoint docs, discovering that aspect ratio and duration are fiddly, and burning five dollars of credits learning that your prompt wording matters more than your settings. A per-generation price with a working preset behind it is a reasonable fee for skipping all of that, especially for people who want one clip for a group chat and never think about it again. Volume users are the ones who should walk.
notes: Thin wrapper, honestly priced thinness, and the wrapper is genuinely the hard part for non-developers.
prompt:
Build a local-only image-to-dance-video tool. Stack: Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, no database, no auth, no telemetry.

In scope:
- One page at / with a drag-and-drop image upload (jpg/png/webp, max 10MB), a preview thumbnail, a duration toggle (8s / 12s), a resolution toggle (480p / 720p), a prompt textarea prefilled with a tuned dance prompt, and a Generate button.
- A server route at /api/generate that uploads the image to the provider and submits an image-to-video job. Use fal.ai as the provider and read FAL_KEY from .env.local. Put the exact model slug in a single MODEL constant at the top of a lib/provider.ts file so it can be swapped in one edit.
- Poll job status from a /api/status/[id] route. Show a status line with elapsed seconds. Do not block the request thread waiting for the render.
- On completion, download the MP4 server-side into ./output/{timestamp}-{id}.mp4 and write a sibling JSON file with the prompt, duration, resolution, model slug and provider job id.
- A gallery section on the same page that reads ./output via a server component and lists finished clips newest first, each with an inline video player and a download link.
- Keep a hardcoded array of 5 dance prompt presets in lib/presets.ts that fill the textarea on click.

Out of scope: user accounts, payments, cloud storage, queues, Docker, tests, analytics, any face swap or likeness feature, any moderation claims.

Requirements:
- Fail loudly: if FAL_KEY is missing, render a red banner on the page instead of throwing at request time.
- Surface provider errors verbatim in the UI, including rejected-input errors, so cost and failures are visible.
- Show an estimated credit cost next to the Generate button, read from a plain constant the user is told to edit after checking current provider rates.
- Write a README with setup steps, where to get an API key, and a one-line warning that the user is responsible for having rights to any image they upload.
- .gitignore must exclude .env.local and ./output.
